key_insight: Multi-agent collaboration is not always better: as language models become more capable, the benefits of teamwork can shrink or even disappear. The paper shows that the best architecture depends on the task and model setup, and a predictive selector can choose well in most held-out cases within the same domain.
problem_solved: This paper addresses the challenge of deciding when to use single-agent versus multi-agent language model systems, since collaboration can sometimes improve performance and sometimes make it worse.
method: Ran a controlled study across 260 multi-agent and single-agent configurations of large language model systems.
Compared performance outcomes to identify conditions where collaboration helps, has no effect, or hurts.
Built a predictive model to recommend the best architecture for a given setup, achieving 87% accuracy on held-out within-domain configurations.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this means multi-agent systems should be chosen strategically rather than assumed to be superior. The results provide a practical way to design more efficient, reliable LLM systems without unnecessary complexity.
visual_elements: Side-by-side comparison chart of single-agent vs. multi-agent performance
Flow diagram showing when collaboration helps, hurts, or is neutral
Grid or heatmap of the 260 tested configurations
Decision-tree or selector icon illustrating the predictive architecture chooser
paper_title: Capable language models can outgrow the benefits of collaboration
paper_authors: Yubin Kim, Ken Gu, Chanwoo Park, Chunjong Park, Samuel Schmidgall
